actions.justification: First mandatory step - obtain comprehensive history to identify chief complaint, symptom onset, prior cardiac history, medications, and risk factors to guide the workup.
Mandatory physical exam to assess for signs of heart failure (JVD, crackles, edema, S3 gallop), volume status, and hemodynamic stability.
Mandatory ECG to identify arrhythmias, ischemia, conduction abnormalities, or LVH that may underlie or contribute to the cardiac presentation.
Mandatory action: BNP/NT-proBNP is essential for diagnosing and assessing severity of heart failure, which is the likely working diagnosis given the clinical context.
Mandatory action: Chest X-ray evaluates for pulmonary congestion, cardiomegaly, and pleural effusions, critical in heart failure workup.
Mandatory action: BMP assesses renal function, electrolytes, and guides safe initiation/titration of heart failure medications such as diuretics and ACE inhibitors.
Mandatory action - CBC is required to evaluate for anemia, infection, or other hematologic abnormalities that may contribute to or complicate heart failure or the working diagnosis.

Mandatory action - TSH is required to evaluate for thyroid dysfunction (hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism) which can be a reversible cause of cardiac dysfunction and must be assessed as part of the workup.
After initial labs and imaging ordered, assessing hemodynamic profile (warm/cold, wet/dry) will guide further management decisions including diuretic therapy and advanced treatment planning.

Assessing LVEF is a critical next step in heart failure workup to guide therapy selection (e.g., HFrEF vs HFpEF), determine eligibility for guideline-directed medical therapy, and assess need for device therapy. Basic labs, BNP, ECG, and CXR have been completed; echocardiographic assessment of LVEF is now the priority.

After or concurrent with LVEF assessment, evaluating ICD indication is important — patients with reduced LVEF (≤35%) despite optimal medical therapy may qualify for primary prevention ICD per ACC/AHA guidelines.

CRT indication assessment is guideline-recommended for patients with HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%), symptomatic heart failure on optimal medical therapy, and QRS duration ≥130ms with LBBB — should be evaluated alongside ICD candidacy.

NYHA functional classification is essential for guiding heart failure management decisions including medication titration, device therapy eligibility, and advanced therapy assessment. Has not yet been completed.
Assessing structural cardiac abnormalities (e.g., valvular disease, wall motion abnormalities) informs etiology and guides treatment planning in heart failure.
Cardiac rehabilitation improves functional capacity and outcomes in stable heart failure patients. Patient vitals are stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), making this an appropriate consideration.

With assessment complete (NYHA class, LVEF, BNP, structural abnormalities, ICD/CRT candidacy all evaluated), the next step is to verify whether guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) has been optimized and for sufficient duration before considering advanced therapies or escalation.

After comprehensive HF workup, evaluate whether this patient meets criteria for advanced heart failure therapies (LVAD, transplant) based on NYHA class, LVEF, and hemodynamic profile already assessed.
Assess for and address volume overload/congestion as part of optimizing GDMT in heart failure management, per standard HF guidelines.
After initial workup and diuretic initiation, confirming that the patient is on optimal guideline-directed medical therapy is the priority next step in heart failure management.
ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI is a cornerstone of HFrEF GDMT. With stable BP (120/80) and no contraindications apparent, initiation or optimization should be considered.
Beta-blocker therapy is mandatory GDMT for HFrEF. HR is 80 and BP is stable, making this an appropriate time to initiate or confirm beta-blocker use.

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone/eplerenone) is indicated in HFrEF patients already on beta-blocker and ACE/ARB/ARNI to reduce mortality and morbidity, provided renal function and potassium are acceptable.
Patient has undergone advanced therapy candidacy assessment; if eligible, initiate formal transplant or LVAD workup to optimize long-term management options.
If resting HR remains ≥70 bpm despite maximally tolerated beta-blocker and patient is in sinus rhythm with reduced EF, ivabradine is guideline-recommended to reduce HF hospitalization.
